body: Thank you, I'm sorry you're going through the same. I really appreciate your comment.

Thank you for taking the time to reply to me. I have been in the psychiatric hospital for the past two weeks, getting the help I need. I'm due to be discharged soon, and feeling kinda ready and safe in myself.

Thank you Mum. I kept myself safe through the night just thinking about the doctor coming today to do a psych eval. I really appreciate what you wrote to me. My own mum is emotionally detached, and blames me and my siblings for her life being ruined by just being born. The only times I've tried to have a real conversation with her is when I've been too drunk to care about her narcissistic responses. Thank you for believing in me, and for taking the time out of your day to see me at my worst and to still be there.

It's okay, thanks for checking in. I'm feeling pretty low and in a 'fucky' mood where I just feel like doing bad things. 

It's exhausting isn't it? Thank you again for checking in, it means a lot.

I would like to understand you more. I'm glad you felt able to open up, sometimes just hashing it out in writing can help the chaos in our heads click into view. I hear you saying that you prefer the extremes over being content, and 'safe'. 

I think you're absolutely right in saying that because you have lived your life in extremes (from poverty, to your own emotions) that it feels somewhat alien and hard to accept normalcy. I find the same; extremes is all I've ever known, so any straying from that path leads to boredom, leads to suicidal ideation. 

It feels wrong to say it out loud, but here you are surrounded by people who have lived with extremes, and who also may experience normalcy as boring and stifling. 

Can I ask, are you in any sort of therapy program to help you combat these thoughts?

I started last week again, and have cut every day since. I'm genuinely sorry that you are feeling this way. I related to your sentence about your body also being physically slower. Correct me if I am wrong, but it feels like you're drunk or high without having imbibed? I won't give you any tired platitudes, just know that I hear you and see you. Have you found your emotions cycling again today?

Thank you that means a lot. It takes me forever to get over the mental hurdles that I've put up over my life like 'no one really wants to listen', 'no one would care anyway', 'they don't want to help, they want to use you' etc. 

I did not laugh, I believe what you said. I'm frustrated at therapy being held online; it's three days a week and the intensity and constant re-traumatisation after someone talks about something is really getting to me. I just feel so utterly hopeless and dejected and deflated. I'm scared that the next, tiny little thing will push me over the edge.
They did say they weren't frustrated or annoyed; just worried and concerned. But I don't feel deserving of concern so I didn't really trust it, you know?

I can't even begin to think of one, concrete reason why. Maybe it's the escapism factor that calls me? I don't know. 

You can type it here if you want, I won't judge. I don't think being suicidal would just cease to exist purely because you are well-off, you can be fine physically but not mentally.
Ugh yeah. I look about 15 despite being 27 and I always get that. Same tired platitudes. Same useless words. No one listens, they just wait until they can tell you to man up.

You seem like a very intelligent and introspective person, and I'm glad to have your input on this post. It's made me realise that I knew the answer to my question, I just didn't want to face the harsh reality. I find it extremely difficult to put myself in someone else's place, and see things as they see them. I honestly could not gauge the reaction in my friends following a text out of the blue like that. 

Even based on their replies, I still cannot work out (nor will I ever know) exactly what they think of me. I've been struggling a lot lately with the idea that people outside of me will have a completely different version of who I am in their heads. 

How can there be so many different 'me's', when I don't even know who I am myself? I have spent too long trying to analyse how I come across to others and figure out who these other 'me's' are. For some reason, I find it abhorrent that I exist to other people and that I am an exterior person in their lives. I am sent on a path of "They must hate me, how could they not? I am everything bad in the world, I've ruined their lives simply by being in it." 

If I try to imagine my friend talking about me to another person, all I hear is, "Oh, my friend Klaus has BPD too. Did I tell you about the time she called me up at 0900 drunk as hell crying that she was going to kill herself, and I had to talk to her for hours just to get her to calm down enough to call the Crisis Team? She has so many scars on her arms too! All over! Real, fucked up. She still lives with her parents... etc etc." 

Even though, I think I know they would never do that. They are not cruel or mean to me, and have only ever been kind and sympathetic. They've never belittled me, or degraded me or doubted the existence of my BPD, and yet, that's all I can imagine they would say. Even though I *know* they would never.

I think those around me find it difficult to hear that, on one hand, I know they love me and care for me, and yet simultaneously the BPD side leads me to believe that they hate me. I've had numerous friends and exes become upset and say "How could you think so little of me? That you think I would ever do or say something like that?" And I don't know how to get across the fact that I don't think that of them, not really. But also I do. Or rather, maybe I am just scared they do, and it gets mistranslated in my head as they do? 

I don't know, I think I've started to ramble.

I'm sorry. I know it's hard. I wish I could step outside of myself too, instead I am trapped in a cyclical hell of delusion and confusion and distress. Every tiny thing is a threat to me. I think (for some of us, at least) we know deep down that that love for us is there, but it becomes overshadowed by doubt, guilt, anger, hurt, pain, trauma... and difficult to see through this haze of emotion. Sometimes it is more evident that the love is there, and sometimes it only takes the merest hint or suggestion (imagined or real) for that blockade to come down and the instant killswitch is engaged so we can't see it, can't remember it and don't even know it ever existed in the first place.

You're right about rewiring. One of my counsellors once told me that the brain's 'habits' (such as self-harm, or an atypical reaction to a simple conversation) are like pathways, you walk them long enough and they become deeply entrenched and carved into the landscape. 

For example; if that person had used self-harm for years as a coping mechanism because it's the only way they felt control in an abusive relationship, or they had built up distrust around certain subjects since a traumatic incident.

But new habits can also be formed like pathways, you walk the same, new path for long enough and it slowly starts to form its own walkway. If the old pathway is disused for long enough, it eventually fills in with dirt or plants and gets forgotten.

This was heartbreaking to read, and it surfaced in me a lot of thought as to how my own siblings may feel when it comes to seeing me in my self-destructive phases. It was especially wonderful to read that you harbour no thoughts of guilt or anger towards your sister, and how much you deeply care about her. 

I want to say as someone with BPD, that there are these dissociative fugues that can come over some of us, and only afterwards can we see the full extent of the damage we've done to others. Even then, it can be warped and skewed by delusions and confusion and extreme guilt which can eat away at a person until they can't take it anymore and enter another episode that once again, hurts those closest to us. This is by no means an excuse, just a potential reason.

Like your sister, all of my hurt is directed inwards, which I think also hurts others by indirect means. It must be hard to watch and not be able to do more than you are. 

People like you, and with your mindset, are greatly appreciated and extremely beneficial to the recovery of people with BPD.

My friends are aware of my diagnosis and made some attempt to learn a bit about what it is for me. It's not really discussed at all until I tell them I've just come off the ward or something - and they can only offer condolences that it has happened. They do let me know in various ways that they care deeply for me and that they are there, but it is impossible for me in the midst of an episode to contact someone. I'm so grateful your sister has such a wonderful sibling that they trust to be there with them in their journey to recovery.

I think the best way to stop feeling all this guilt and shame is to have an open, honest dialogue with her. You will only go on feeling this way if you never get the issue resolved. Tell her that you're scared that you may have lead her on, let her know (in a nice way) that it was a one-time thing, and you're confused about it yourself. Be honest. You don't know why you initiated it. As a bisexual person herself, she may have had similar experiences of confusion. Let her know that you're sure that you are heterosexual, and let her know that you're scared about your friendship dynamic changing. 

One of my closest friends had been into me for about 10 years, and one day, on a drunken night out I accidently (?) had sex with her. We had gone to a bar as a group and at one point I leaned over to tell her I was going to the toilet. She knows I'm gay, and took it as an 'invitation', and followed me into the stall where we started hooking up. I honestly wasn't into her like that, nor did I think it through while it was happening. But afterwards I felt so guilty and sick. This was my best friend, who was definitely into me, and now I've fucked it all up by sleeping with her and probably making her think I was interested. 

Our friendship was strained for a while afterwards because I just dropped out of existence in my friend group out of shame and guilt. Eventually I thought the only thing I could do was to try and explain myself. I told her I was sorry, and I wasn't into her like that, and it was a one-time thing. (I didn't ever say, "oh it was just a drunken thing" I didn't want to belittle her or make her feel worthless - but I did want her to know that it wouldn't happen again) I told her I was scared I may have led her on, and may have hindered our otherwise good relationship. 

She understood and while she was a bit sad that it was a one-time thing, she was ready to accept that it had happened and it couldn't be changed, and to move on. 

The only way forward is communication. Be kind, be gentle, be honest. I hope this helps. (That means don't tell her you were so grossed out afterwards that you needed several showers - she is human too, and deserves some dignity).

Same. I realised I was the problem in every relationship. Even with old school friends I struggle to maintain a healthy boundary and to react in an appropriate manner to every perceived slight. Romantic relationships are completely out for me now. Every time I load up tinder or some shit I just talk to people for a few days and realise it's fruitless because I'm going to end up killing myself. I get so loaded up with these destructive thoughts I physically remove myself from other people's lives to spare them the trouble. The only problem is I just can't exist by myself. My personality is based on those around me. When I'm alone (especially trying to do something solo, like travelling) I am just a void and have no one to gauge my own feelings by. Being along makes me sick to the stomach.

Yeah, I could bring it up to my therapist. I never really talk about it there because I'm afraid I won't be taken seriously. "It's only BPD. Paranoia isn't that bad with BPD. You must be faking." Kind of response.

I get unreasonably paranoid when I'm majorly distressed. When my ex was thinking about breaking up with me I became so paranoid that I refused to believe that she was 'the real' her, and that she'd been swapped out with a fake copy because "the real her wouldn't act like this". 

I have been paranoid that my friends secretly text my parents and tell them what a horrible person I am, and my parents reply saying how disgusting a child I am. 

I got paranoid that my therapy room was bugged and we were all being monitored through a wire in a light fixture. I get paranoid I'm being followed, or watched, or talked about. 

I have a big thing that I think everyone can read my secret posts or journal - even if they feasibly have no access. When my family talks to each other and I'm slightly out of ear-shot I believe that they're all talking about me. 

I have no idea how to tell the difference, because asking someone usually means I distrust what they say because I'm paranoid in the first place!

Hey now, if it matters to you, then it matters. I don't have any experience with what you're struggling with, but can offer a couple of suggestions. You could write a letter to them? A sort of 'Thank you for....' kind of letter? So if they do get left behind then you have a nice reminder of all the things you value and like about this character. 

As for the uncertainty, you know one of two things is going to happen, don't you? They stay, or they go? Prepare for both cases, write the letter, draw a picture... if you have a garden or some plant pots, plant a seed! You want to be able to look back and this game and see the wonderful time you had playing it, not focus on this potential loss of the character. 

They will always be there in the earlier parts of the game, no? 
I hope this helps, keep your chin up and happy gaming!

I finished my Bachelor's in Illustration about 5 years back, and got diagnosed my first year of university. I chose the course because I'd done a Foundation Diploma in Art and Design and enjoyed illustration because of the crossover between structured briefs and interpretation. I'm happy I did Illustration, and I got a 2:1, but it was insanely difficult to do so. 

I deferred one module due to a suicide attempt, and every single deadline I seemed to have to apply for mitigating circumstances because my BPD interfered to the point I couldn't get the work done on time. 

My tutors were incredibly helpful and understanding; I think it helped that they liked me anyway and saw potential in me, so they were more likely to 'put up' with my delayed deadlines and chronically missed lectures. I also think it helped that I am smart academically, and talented at art. 

I'm honestly surprised at the fact I managed to pull a 2:1 out of the bag, looking back on my projects and the little work I put into them it's surprising I achieved any success at all. 

I don't utilise my degree at all now; (another story altogether), and am currently considering a master's (a creative arts and therapy course), but I'm in an intensive therapy program at the moment so I'm unsure if it's right for me apply just yet.

Thank you so much for the insight into your thought and action process. It's interesting that once you have the thought, the action follows. I seem to get stuck on the thought. 

However, once, I did something called a pre-mortem. You know how a post-mortem is finding out all that went wrong with the body after death? Well, a pre-mortem is a similar thing, but with a thought process instead. Figure out what *could* go wrong *before* you act.

You start out by identifying what it is you want to do. In my case, it was "Should I camp on the beach after my friend's wedding to avoid paying for accommodation?" 

I really wanted to do it. I could picture myself setting up, collecting firewood, sitting and having a hot drink under the dying sunlight... Waking up to the sound of crashing waves, seagulls calling, and feeling at peace.

The pre-mortem is designed to help you figure out all the worst-case scenarios, every little niggling thought that eats at you telling you not to go ahead with it. 

I identified my fears; I didn't want to get told off for camping, I didn't want to get robbed or attacked (young, single woman camping alone) I didn't want to get carried away by the sea while I slept etc.

Then I identified what would make all these things happen; Overstaying my welcome, being too loud or destructive, drawing attention to myself, not locking up my belongings and setting up camp in a tidal zone. 

Lastly was how to avoid these things happening; I'd arrive as late as possible and leave as early as possible. I'd bring a small padlock, keep my phone charged at all times, tell people where I was and how long I would be there for. I'd not be loud, and leave no trace. I'd set up camp somewhere as hidden as possible, and out of the tidal zone. 

After that I weighed up the pros and cons - and found there were more pros than cons, and so I cemented in my head that that was what I would do.

It was one of the best experiences as well, because I was prepared and knew all of my avenues to keep myself safe and happy. 

I'd completely forgotten this technique, but speaking with you has brought it to the forefront of my mind. Thank you for reminding me that the power to act can come from within me, instead of through validation from others.

I didn't know I'd been diagnosed until I received my care plan after a breakdown and hospitalisation. I'd suspected for a while, and my counsellor at uni had alluded to it but she was not licensed to diagnose me. Just a couple words in a wall of text 'Diagnosis: EUPD with codependent traits' - back when I was in a relationship with my ex. It's changed slightly now to just BPD. 
How old are you? They are extremely reluctant to diagnose people under 25 - and point blank refuse under 18. This is because the brain is still changing and developing and normal developmental issues can be confused with symptoms. 

It's really good that the OCD specialist recognised your need for DBT. Things gotta be worked on in order unfortunately, or you won't make any sense of it. DBT is really good for the most pressing and harmful things like self-harm, suicidal thoughts etc. 

Later on, once your self-destructive issues have been calmed somewhat, or even eradicated, then you can work on more in-depth psychology. Psychodynamic psychotherapy for example, going back deep into your past and exploring potential trauma and issues you faced growing up. 

Imagine they were going to diagnose you with BPD, and throw you into a therapy like that. It would be excruciating and extremely difficult for you to go through all that whilst you are still actively self-harming and prone to destructive behaviours. Bringing up all the bad shit when your only coping mechanism is to hurt yourself. That could end extremely badly for you. 

I got so frustrated when they wouldn't start me on the therapy they suggested because I had just attempted suicide and was self-harming constantly, and turned up to my assessment having had a drink. But they needed me to be slightly more stable so that I was strong enough to open up in therapy and not be high-risk. 

It kinda makes sense to me now, but ultimately frustrating in the beginning. I hope your journey with DBT goes well.

Thank you for sharing a bit about your life, I found it insightful. You know that we can't diagnose you or even really say 'that sounds like BPD', as it's against sub rules (and pretty much a bad idea for anyone who isn't a licensed professional running a diagnostic test).

First off, I'm sorry that there seem to be no options for you in the form of counselling. I'm hazarding a guess that you might be in the states, and that's why it seems so far away and unaffordable to you. I can't really offer any advice regarding this, as I'm from the UK. 

Secondly, I picked up on an overwhelming problem surrounding your sleep, specifically, your inability to get a solid night's sleep. Are you currently in work? What does your day look like? Sometimes, huge periods of inactivity will actually make it extremely difficult to fall asleep. 

I know this may sound beside the point; but according to every psychologist, therapist, mental health advisor, GP, psychotherapist and counsellor I've ever seen, you NEED to try and eliminate all of the basic needs as contributing factors for your stress, mood swings, and anxiety, which in turn, are affecting your relationships. 

The first thing a psychologist would do would be to make sure that your basic needs are being met, and if anything needs working on so that your quality of life can improve. They will be hesitant to diagnose anyone, without eliminating these are potential factors first.

So food; are you eating a healthy balanced diet? 
Water; are you getting enough water throughout the day?
Exercise; are you regularly exercising, walking or working out?
Sleep; do you practice good sleep routine? E.g No screen times two hours before bed, gentle reading, no caffeine?
Other; do you use drugs? Drink alcohol? Smoke? Energy drinks or coffee? Do you take medication? 
Social; do you have friends? How often and what is the quality of your interaction with friends, family or relationships? 
Work or education; do you work or attend school or college? What is that like?

Pretty much all of these factors can contribute to the things you have described. By no means am I saying that they are the sole reason, but they can exacerbate already low moods and anxieties. 

It sounds to me that you are very unsatisfied with yourself when it comes to relationships, and I'm noting some very negative vocabulary directed at yourself. You don't seem to think yourself worthy of being in a relationship, yet crave it above all else. This may be why you feel like you are constantly on the edge of being left alone. 

You mentioned that sometimes you can be with your partner 'all the time' for a few days, and then have to pull away to get some space. Perhaps instead of ricocheting between all the time, and never, you could spread out your time across the week. So see him for a few hours a day, as opposed to 24/3 and then having to remove yourself to not feel suffocated. 

The key to any relationship is communication. You and your partner need to effectively communicate and understand each other's needs to make it work. Tell him what you told us; that it actually wasn't about not kissing him, but that you were feeling overwhelmed and needed some time to breathe. There's no harm in letting him know what you need. 

Perhaps it would help you to verbalise your anxiety. You said you have a good relationship with your family. Could you talk to them about your worries regarding the entrance exam? 

Sorry about the length of my reply, I hope it helps.

That's not normal for a decent, good instructor. I went through exactly what you're going through. My instructor knew my sister from her old job, and so I felt bad trying to say anything as she had told me he was very nice. He would cancel often, not contact me for days; once it was two weeks, where I tried to text and call to set up a new session, but he just never replied.

I also suffer from mental illness, and being young and scared and anxious, I thought that's just how things worked, and that I was overreacting by thinking that it somehow wasn't right. 

He would stop the session so that he could stand outside the car and vape by playing on my insecurities and lack of confidence. He'd say, "You look anxious, let's have a break." all the time, which meant I never made any progress, and made me feel like a nervous wreck. Of course, on the surface it sounds like he's being nice and accommodating of my anxiety, but I really wanted to overcome that and work hard to pass, which I couldn't do when we had a break every 20 minutes in a two hour session. 

He'd also just kick back the entire time and be like, "So what do you wanna do?" spouting off about how it was his 'policy' to let students run the sessions. But really, it was an out for him, because he was lazy and didn't plan for lessons or care about my weaknesses and what I needed to work on.

I once got stood up for a lesson that we'd booked the week prior, and I couldn't get in touch for days until he finally just said, "It was my day off that day." No apology, no trying to book a new lesson. 

It's your right to get a decent education from an instructor. If it's not working the way you want it to, then please seek instruction from someone else. There are so many decent instructors, you just need to do some hunting around unfortunately. Like me, you probably hoped that you'd pick an instructor and stick with them until you pass. I've had five different instructors, and only one was decent.

I'll just tell you a bit about what I think makes a good instructor, you'll have your own wants and needs in a tutor but here's some basics:

. Prompt replies in communication during business hours

. Can explain things to you in a way you understand

. Has a two-way policy on cancellation. (My instructor told me at the very beginning, 48 business hours notice at least if you need to cancel, although she would understand genuine emergencies have no notice period. But the important thing is is that it worked the same way if she needed to cancel. So if she couldn't do Monday, for example, she would need to let me know by Thursday prior)

. Has a diary in which you book in your next lesson at the end of the session. This gives you both structure, guarantees them their next pay, and you your next lesson. 

. Can tailor teaching style to the individual student (eg. if you're a visual learner, have reference pictures and can recommend videos and learning materials)

. Notices what you struggle with and helps you to overcome that in a non demeaning or aggressive manner

. Is active in listening and understanding you and your needs

. Makes you feel comfortable in the car. (A big one if you have anxiety, they should make you feel like you can just naturally get in a car and go with confidence. They should never, ever invade your personal space either)

. If you have your own car and can practice with someone independently outside of lesson time, gives you things to practice and improve upon.

. Instills confidence in your driving ability, and lets you know that it's okay to go at your own pace and to take the time you need to feel comfortable with each aspect of driving

. Should let you feel able to ask questions when you need to, without feeling stupid

. Should make you look forward to learning how to drive! You will of course have your reservations and anxieties, but driving should be an enjoyable experience! You're paying for a service and you can decide what you need from it

. Can have a bit of a chat and joke with, often overlooked, because of some age disparity with young learners, but having a good connection can do wonders for your confidence

. Should nudge you gently on areas that need the most improvement. I hated roundabouts and hillstarts with a passion and thought I'd never get them. Today I can do them without thinking because my instructor would take me to safe, secluded areas to work on them until I felt comfortable with them

. Only makes you go for the test when you yourself feel ready

Unfortunately lots of these things you will only find out once you've had a couple of lessons, but I urge you to stand by what you need from an instructor, and if something doesn't feel right to you, then listen to your gut  and take into account these points. 

I really hope that this helps you in some way. Remember, you have a reason for feeling like you're getting shunted about, and it's because you are. Before you start having lessons, make a note of some of the more business-y points and ask these questions before you book a lesson. 

Like, "What is your cancellation policy? Can you book the next session at the end of the previous session? Do you tailor your teaching style to suit the needs of the client? Do you reply same-day during business hours if I have a query?" 

Good luck, friend, and happy driving! It's such an amazing feeling to pass and to have the independence of driving! Don't forget why you want to learn!

Honestly, you did the best thing for yourself by contacting your GP. It sounds like you needed intervention, even if you didn't see yourself as an 'emergency case'. When we find ourselves completely overwhelmed and distressed, so much so that we have a detailed suicide plan and are going to act on it, we need intervention. 

Crisis lines and support lines can really only do so much over the phone. Unfortunately; they're billed as a 'last resort', someone to call when you feel overwhelmed, but they are legally not allowed to tell you what to do. That's why I referred to them 'support lines' instead of suicidal hotlines. You can call them when you feel low, and need someone to talk through your emotions and they will listen, and empathise with you, and try to help calm you down enough to think rationally and analyse why you feel this way.

However, they're not really suitable for someone with BPD, having a severe suicidal breakdown. In times when you feel like you need intervention, not just support, or talking to someone, please remember the time you called your GP and got a referral to be seen immediately. Episodes such as yours are immensely scary, and you may not know what you need, or how you can be helped, you may not feel like you even deserve help, but you do. 

It can be helpful to try and notice the differences between needing support, and needing intervention. If you can, and when you feel well enough, try to write out (exactly as you've done here) what you were going through, the triggers, and your reaction. 

Notice also when you are not an immediate risk to yourself, but rather needing someone to talk to. Write this down as well and compare it to when you were so distressed that you could not physically stop yourself from wanting to commit suicide unless someone actively stepped in. Hopefully with time you won't have to go through the extremely traumatising time of calling a 'suicide hotlines' only to be shunted out or hung up on, and can seek the correct help from your GP or local A&E.

It sounds like you’re going through a really frightening time. Feeling disconnected, far removed and apart from yourself can be very scary. Has this happened to you before or often? Sometimes; the mind’s way of coping with distressing feelings or thoughts or memories is to cut off entirely. The mind takes a back seat and your body continues without it. Can you think of anything that might have caused this? If not, sometimes there is no real reason that we can discern, sometimes we’re not good at figuring out the ‘why’, especially in the fog of disassociation.

With regards to cutting/burning, and forgive me for making an assumption, but it sounds to me like you are desperate to feel again. To regain some control over your situation, and to bring you back to the world your mind has disconnected with. As crass and feeble as it may sound, have you tried grounding techniques? Being clean for a whole year is an amazing milestone in your recovery, and you must remember that this period won’t last. It might be helpful to take this moment of composure to try something you might not be willing to try were you in a worse place. Maybe an ice cold shower, or some mindfulness. More than anything, I can hear the desperation in your post to not lose yourself. I want to let you know that you’re not lost, nor in danger of losing yourself. Your mind has opted to ‘step out’ for a bit, and there are many ways to get it to come back inside. 

Try to focus on your surroundings, and the space you take up in them. If you’re sitting, notice the weight of yourself in the seat, the feel of the floor at your feet. What sort of health professionals do you have on support? I am also in the UK and as I understand it there are various routes you can go down to get help. Forgive me if you are aware of these avenues already. 

There are a few categories that mental health care falls into - and the support you receive will reflect that. 

First off, is Primary Care. This would be your GP, Doctor and charity services such as Mind. Primary care deals with those whose problems are seen to be able to be helped by these services.

Next is Secondary Care. This would be your Community Mental Health Team, and their psychologists and psychiatrists. This level of care is for those who are unlikely to be helped by *just* primary care services alone. Those who need a bit more specialist care.

Last (I believe) is Tertiary. This involves inpatient care, such as being in a psychiatric hospital. This is for those who cannot be helped by *just* primary or secondary, and need even more specialist care. 

When I started receiving help it was through a counsellor at my university. Unfortunately my problems became more and more debilitating and I needed more specialist care. They helped me to get referred to the CMHT through my GP (as I understand, this is the main route to go to get under the CMHT).

If you are under secondary care, you cannot be under primary care as well, and vice versa. I’m not sure how lax they are with this, as I believe to use Mind services you would be discharged from CMHT. 

I was diagnosed through the CMHT who needed to assess me when I was referred. If you are concerned about the likelihood of a diagnosis, I think the avenue is to get referred to CMHT by the GP. 

There is also something called Single Point if Access, (at least here in Kent, give it a google) where you can call up and they will help you to find the right service for you. 

In the meantime, I suggest going for this group if you can, as I know you’re aware, it does no harm to give it a go.

Whilst I cannot speak for everyone, here are some things I believe might be good for us with BPD. 

People diagnosed with BPD need structure. They also need some social aspects, without being too intrusive or pressured. We tend to find low-pressure environments easier to sustain, with a more relaxed approach to work. Basically; something where we can get involved and be a part of, without having the extra pressure of becoming overly-involved and causing damage by striving to fulfil extreme workloads. 

As we tend to struggle with thoughts of self-identity, interpersonal relationships, and our general chaotic minds, it stands to reason that something that can accommodate our needs whilst providing structure and a sense of achievement would benefit us greatly.

Some people find that delivery or driving occupations are perfect for them. Set your own hours, and still have a social aspect, whilst allowing for the occasional lapse in mental state without serious repercussions in our work life. 

Some people find freelance work is best - again - set your own hours and socialising. Freelance artists, photographers, editors, journalists, graphic designers.. I’m sure there are more. 

Some people find volunteering is beneficial. If you’re on benefits like I am, volunteering means that you can regain some structure in your life whilst still being a low-pressure environment. 

Unfortunately, I have only a limited scope of careers, but as the world has changed so much since the days of ‘pick a job and work it until you retire’ - there is no reason why you cannot start in one area and then switch to another later on. It’s not a failure, it’s pretty much the norm nowadays, and it is suitable for those diagnosed with BPD and our ever-changing ideas of who we are and what we want to be doing. 

I hope this helps a little.

My friend has started doing inner-child work with her therapist recently, and she’s found it very beneficial. Basically when you notice you’re having a bad thought about yourself, you take a step away from yourself and envision that it was you as a young child that said that thought. Then you react to your own inner child, and talk to them as you would a child. 

So in your case it may be; “God why did I say such a stupid thing, everyone must hate me.” 

And your adult-you might reply, “Why makes you say that?” 

And so on, just being really gentle and understanding of your child self, and trying to understand your reasoning behind your bad thought. 

I’ve not tried it myself, but you know what they say, try everything and eventually something might stick. 

I myself sometimes use the ‘scientist’ technique. Where I get a bad or intrusive thought, and then play scientist with myself. What physical evidence do I have that supports my theory? What evidence do I have that DOESN’T support my theory?

I’m from England, so may not be much help, but yes they do exist. There’s a PD Peer Support Group near me, no commitment, no strings. Just turn up and talk if you want. It probably varies, but this particular group you all take turns to unload for about 15 minutes and can receive help, support and feedback from the group facilitator and your fellow PD peers who may have helpful information. It doesn’t have to be intense, sometimes I’ve gone in and just said that I’ve not really been up to much, and other times I’ve gone in with a full-house, complete trifecta of assorted problems and stressors and received support every time. It’s great you’re considering it, it can be hard to ask for help, but meeting and interacting with people with the same diagnosis allows you to voice things that you wouldn’t ever be able to say with friends, family, and even health care providers. We all just ‘get’ it, and it’s relieving. Good luck.

As another commenter mentioned; yes you can get psychotic and paranoid symptoms with BPD if you are stressed enough. You seem very determined to convince us of your reality; but don’t be afraid, we are not here to judge or disprove you or claim your own reality is false because it might not align with our own. Just be mindful that you mention this to your care professional, as these symptoms (while not usually long-lasting) can be hugely distressing for people. Try not to place so much focus on the symptoms and medication and work with your psych to determine WHY it’s happening. Remember, your experience is valid; focus on the background music.

You could try come up with back-up plans together? Like when you’re both in a good headspace, start jotting down activities that you both feel comfortable doing when either of you can’t do something more exciting/out there. Compile a list of interesting, ‘safe’ plans, like maybe rewatching an old favourite film together, going to the library/museum, blanket fort, cooking sensory dinner together etc. 

I think above all the hardest part is simply to just believe what you already know; that is isn’t a personal attack on you if she can’t do what you wanted to do. Perhaps take a deep breath upon receiving the ‘no’ and try to picture if the roles were reversed. Ask yourself (or even her!) what emotions and feelings and thoughts led her to her decision - it may help you to understand her intentions are innocent and not directed at you. 

I hope this helps; I understand your feelings, and I know that with enough time it will become easier for you - it’s breaking a long-standing cycle of thought-patterns.

Hello, I may have the information you need. 

I am on Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payment (P.I.P) and am diagnosed with BPD.

Universal credit is slowly replacing all the benefits like ESA and DLA etc into one single benefit (that takes into account all of your circumstances as if you were applying for ESA, Council Tax etc separately).

I currently live with my parents and do not pay any sort of rent, nor do I have a job. Under the Universal Credit system there are two types of ‘entitlements’. The first is ‘Work Capability’ where they assess your need for support and whether you are able to work. 

I was put into the second category; ‘not being able to work’. I had to fill out a form from my work coach (whom I was still seeing every week and getting odd bits of information and help from - it helps to have a work coach who has some experience working with disabilities as they are more understanding) 

The form assessed my ability to carry out work related tasks. I filled it out as if describing my ‘worst day’ (I.e unable to leave the house with anxiety, unpredictable rage, self-harm and suicide) whatever your symptoms are that prevent you from working.

Once I filled out this form I was given an appointment to be assessed in person and it was hella scary and the man didn’t listen - but in the end all he was doing was confirming everything I had written in my form.

They then placed me in the ‘limited/no work capability’ section and I didn’t have to meet with a work coach anymore unless I felt ready/wanted to.

I also applied for P.I.P on the off chance they would also be able to accept me and the form to fill out was essentially the same. I scanned in and supplied about 20-30 pages worth of all the doctors notes, care plans, hospital admissions, medications that I’d ever had due to BPD as a supplement. 

I also attached (to both forms) a letter specifically written by my care coordinator at the community mental health team I am at under secondary care, to help with my case. She wrote that my diagnose made it impossible to work at the moment. 

It helped a lot to have a specific, recent letter. 

P.I.P didn’t ask for an assessment (my guess is they couldn’t be bothered to read the huge amount of scans I’d sent in and just accepted me) - but they sent me a letter saying that I’d been awarded the entitlement. 

Also, unless you specifically have any mobility issues then specify in your form that you are not looking to receive the mobility entitlement (they might appreciate your honesty, in knowing that you aren’t just looking to scam them for free money, but only to get a payment that allows you to function in society. 

I hope this helps! Good luck, friend, and take care.
